title: Lesson 10: Special Multiplication
subtopics: By one more than the one before
First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
learningGoals: Recognize and apply several special multiplication patterns faster than the general method.
Choose the correct shortcut from the structure of the numbers instead of forcing one method everywhere.
Keep place value correct when blocks, complements, and carries are part of the method.
coreIdeas: Special multiplication works because the numbers carry a visible pattern that the board can expose quickly.
Most shortcuts split the answer into left and right blocks, so digit width and carries must be watched carefully.
Mental speed improves when the learner first spots the pattern, then performs a short sequence of reliable steps.

workedExamples.method: Keep 5 and 2 on the outside and place 5 + 2 in the middle.
Use one more than the one before: 4 x 5 gives 20 and 3 x 7 gives 21, so the answer is 2021.
Reduce 763 by one for the left part and use all from 9 and the last from 10 for the right part.
Average 30 and difference 1 give 30 squared minus 1 squared.

starterPractice: Warm-up: multiply 23 by 11 and explain why the sum goes in the middle.
Guided: solve 43 x 47 by finding the left block and right block separately.
Independent: use reduce-by-one and complements to solve 89 x 99.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting Special Multiplication.
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 10: familiar. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Recognize and apply several special multiplication patterns faster than the general method.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in Special Multiplication with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.
A quick review prompt decides whether the learner advances or repeats.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10 to 20 XP per exercise group based on the step position in the lesson path.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak visible on every step and protect it with immediate retries instead of long explanations.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each exercise group has one badge focus tied to the subtopic being learned.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Short praise, points pulse, and progress-bar movement after every correct response.

reviewLoop.trigger: If the learner answers incorrectly, hesitates, or shows low confidence, reopen the same pattern with one smaller follow-up.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Use the micro-practice line as the first repair loop before advancing.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the learner can answer the checkpoint and complete one try in the same subtopic.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Weak steps should return in the next session as review cards before new content.

uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: The learner should see mission progress, the current question, and the main action buttons without long vertical scrolling.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise A: Multiplication by 11 for two-digit numbers
sessionFlow.coachHook: To multiply a two-digit number by eleven, copy the outside digits and place their sum in the middle, carrying if needed.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 52 x 11, copy 5 and 2 to the outside, then reveal the middle sum 5 + 2.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Multiplication by 11 for two-digit numbers is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The answer keeps the first and last digits of 52.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find 23 x 11 and 61 x 11 by saying the middle digit before the full answer.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise B: Multiplication by 11 for longer numbers
sessionFlow.coachHook: For a longer number multiplied by eleven, keep the first and last digits and fill each inside position with the sum of neighboring digits.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 234 x 11, keep 2 and 4 on the ends, then fill the middle places with 2 + 3 and 3 + 4.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Multiplication by 11 for longer numbers is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The first and last digits remain the same.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Compute 423 x 11 and 777 x 11 by filling the inside digits from left to right.

sessionFlow.subtopic: By one more than the one before
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise C: By one more than the one before
sessionFlow.coachHook: When the front parts are the same and the ending parts add to ten or a hundred, multiply the common front by one more and place the product of the endings on the right.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 43 x 47, split it into front 4 and endings 3 and 7, then compute 4 x 5 and 3 x 7.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. By one more than the one before is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The final digits must add to 10 here.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Use the same rule on 62 x 68 and 204 x 206.

sessionFlow.coachHook: To multiply by a row of nines, reduce the number by one for the left part and use all from nine and the last from ten for the right part.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 763 x 999, subtract one from 763 for the left side, then complement 763 for the right side.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Multiplication by nines is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: There will be a left part and a right part.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Work 89 x 99 and 778 x 999 using left part first, then right part.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Two quick multiplication shortcuts work well here: first-by-first-last-by-last for matching endings, and square-the-average minus the square of the difference for centered pairs.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 27 x 87 and 29 x 31 side by side, with one board half for each method.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: We choose the method that matches the number pattern.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find 69 x 49 with the first-last method and 28 x 32 with the average method.

sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?

sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The trick is to notice the special number inside the product.

screenplay.teacherLine: Multiplying by eleven is a place-value pattern, not a long multiplication question.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 52 x 11 and keep space for a three-digit answer.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The answer keeps the first and last digits of 52.

screenplay.teacherLine: The outer digits stay five and two, and the middle digit is their sum, five plus two.
screenplay.boardAction: Fill in 5 _ 2, then write 5 + 2 = 7.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
screenplay.fallbackHint: That gives 572.

screenplay.teacherLine: So 52 times 11 is 572, and the board shows why the sum appears in the middle.
screenplay.boardAction: Box 572 and underline the middle 7.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Outside digits stay fixed; the middle is a sum.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now try 58 times 11, where the middle sum creates a carry.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 5 + 8 = 13 beside 58 x 11.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The 3 stays in the middle and the 1 carries left.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: state the two-digit-by-11 rule in one sentence.
screenplay.boardAction: Leave copy outside digits plus sum middle on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does fifty-two times eleven become five hundred seventy-two?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Keep the outer digits and put their sum in the middle, carrying if needed.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That rule covers both easy and carry cases.

screenplay.teacherLine: The same eleven-pattern extends naturally to three or more digits.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 234 x 11 with a four-digit answer frame 2 _ _ 4.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The first and last digits remain the same.

screenplay.teacherLine: The next digit is two plus three, and the next is three plus four.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 + 4 = 7 into the two gaps.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
screenplay.fallbackHint: That produces 2574.

screenplay.teacherLine: For 777 times 11, the sums are 14 and 14, so carries must be passed leftward.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 7 14 14 7 and then convert it to 8547.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Carries are handled exactly as in ordinary addition.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now fill the inside digits for 423 times 11 before saying the whole answer.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 4 _ _ 3 with helper sums 4 + 2 and 2 + 3.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The inner sums are 6 and 5.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what changes when the neighboring sums are two-digit numbers?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave 14 -> carry 1 marked above the earlier example.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the neighboring-digit sums create 2574 from 234 x 11?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Carry the tens left just like addition.
screenplay.fallbackHint: The pattern stays the same; only the carry handling changes.

screenplay.subtopic: By one more than the one before
screenplay.teacherLine: This method works when the left part matches and the right parts complete a base.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 43 x 47 and circle the common 4, then circle 3 and 7.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does 43 x 47 become 2021?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The final digits must add to 10 here.

screenplay.subtopic: By one more than the one before
screenplay.teacherLine: Multiply four by one more than itself, which is five, to get the left part twenty.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 4 x 5 = 20 on the left side of the answer.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does 43 x 47 become 2021?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Now the right side comes from the final digits.

screenplay.subtopic: By one more than the one before
screenplay.teacherLine: Then multiply three by seven to get twenty-one, so the whole answer is 2021.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 3 x 7 = 21 and join 20 | 21 into 2021.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does 43 x 47 become 2021?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The right side must keep two digits.

screenplay.subtopic: By one more than the one before
screenplay.teacherLine: Apply the same pattern to 62 times 68 and say the left block before the full answer.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 6 x 7 and 2 x 8 as the two mini-calculations.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does 43 x 47 become 2021?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Left block 42, right block 16.

screenplay.subtopic: By one more than the one before
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what do you do if the ending product has only one digit, like zero-nine?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave a note saying keep the right block width.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does 43 x 47 become 2021?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Write a leading zero so the block has the correct number of digits.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Place value must be preserved on the right.

screenplay.teacherLine: A product with nines can be split into two linked pieces.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 763 x 999 and draw a slash in the answer space.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
screenplay.fallbackHint: There will be a left part and a right part.

screenplay.teacherLine: First reduce 763 by one, giving 762 for the left part.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 763 - 1 = 762 on the left of the slash.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This is by one less than the one before.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now complement 763 to get 237, so the full answer is 762 slash 237, meaning 762237.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 999-complement of 763 as 237 and join the two parts.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The right part has the same number of digits as the original number.

screenplay.teacherLine: Use the same method for 89 times 99.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 89 - 1 and complement of 89 with blanks.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Left part 88, right part 11.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: why do we pad with zeros when the row of nines is longer than the number?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave 01867 underlined from the text explanation.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do reduce-by-one and complement together create the answer for 763 x 999?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Because the complement must use the full width of the nines.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Width matters on the right block.

screenplay.subtopic: First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
screenplay.teacherLine: Different products invite different shortcuts, so we compare two useful patterns side by side.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 27 x 87 on the left and 29 x 31 on the right.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: We choose the method that matches the number pattern.

screenplay.subtopic: First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
screenplay.teacherLine: For 27 times 87, the first digits add to ten and the last digits match, so the left part is 2 x 8 + 7 and the right part is 7 x 7.
screenplay.boardAction: Compute 16 + 7 = 23 and 49, then combine them as 2349.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This is first by first and last by last.

screenplay.subtopic: First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
screenplay.teacherLine: For 29 times 31, the average is 30 and the difference is 1, so 30 squared minus 1 squared is 899.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Average method is square of average minus square of difference.

screenplay.subtopic: First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
screenplay.teacherLine: Now use the average method on 28 times 32.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 30^2 - 2^2 with blanks for the numbers.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Average 30, difference 2.

screenplay.subtopic: First by the first and the last by the last, and using the average
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what pattern tells you to use the first-last method instead of the average method?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave matching last digits and fronts sum to 10 in a box.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do you decide between first-by-first-last-by-last and the average method?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Use first-last when last digits match and first digits add to 10.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Use average when the numbers sit equally around a convenient center.

screenplay.teacherLine: Certain numbers repeat or expand in a predictable way, and a disguised factor can reveal them.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 23 x 101 and 24 x 37 as two examples.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The trick is to notice the special number inside the product.

screenplay.teacherLine: Twenty-three times 101 simply repeats 23 to make 2323, because it is 23 hundreds plus 23 ones.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Products with 101, 1001, and similar numbers often repeat the number.

screenplay.teacherLine: For 24 times 37, notice that 3 times 37 is 111, so 24 times 37 is 8 times 111, which is 888.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The hard-looking product becomes a very easy one.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now spot the special number inside 62 times 39.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 62 x 39 = 2 x 31 x 3 x 13 with the pairing blank.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?
screenplay.fallbackHint: 31 x 13 is 403, then multiply 403 by 6.

screenplay.teacherLine: Final checkpoint: when do you pause and look for a disguised factor before multiplying directly?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave 101, 201, 111, 403 listed in a side column.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does spotting a special factor change the multiplication problem before you compute?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: When the factors can be regrouped into a known special number.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Recognition is the speed step here.

teachingFlowStages.intent: Show that a product can often be solved by structure recognition instead of general multiplication.
Explain each shortcut as a repeatable board routine with clear left-right or carry logic.
Demonstrate x11, one-more-than-before, x9s, average, and special-number examples.
Have the learner name the pattern first, then execute the method.
Mix straightforward and disguised cases so recognition becomes part of the skill.
Verify that carries, right-block width, and complements were handled correctly.
Require the learner to explain why a chosen shortcut fits a given pair of numbers.
